newsitem.title: USA: White House treading water on Bosnia force.
newsitem.headline: White House treading water on Bosnia force.

text.p: Anxious to avoid bruising President Bill Clinton's prospects for re-election on Nov. 5, the administration is busily treading water in a tide that appears likely to sweep U.S. troops back to Bosnia next year.

Defence Secretary William Perry and other officials stress repeatedly that Clinton has made no decision on the touchy issue of committing U.S. soldiers for any follow-on to a NATO-led force of 50,000 now being withdrawn from Bosnia.

But with Germany, France, Turkey, Russia and others virtually committed to an expected new force, and allied pressure growing for U.S. participation, the fence-sitting has sparked Republican charges that Clinton is misleading voters, many of whom feel Bosnia is a "European problem".

Analysts agree that the White House and Pentagon probably concluded months ago that a new NATO-led force should include U.S. troops, but fear that any early signal could chip at Clinton's wide pre-election lead over Republican Bob Dole.

Dole says he would not order U.S. troops back to Bosnia to replace the 15,000 American soldiers now being withdrawn with the NATO-led implementation force (IFOR) nearly a year after the Dayton accords.

"The White House is dancing around it. They have already made the decision" to send troops back, said Richard Perle, an Assistant Defence Secretary under former Republican President Ronald Reagan now with the American Enterprise Institute.

"What the administration is stuck with here is that they swore up and down when troops were first sent that one year would be enough. Everybody knew it wouldn't be enough and, of course, it wasn't," Perle told Reuters.

Bruce Pirnie of the Rand Corporation, another private think tank, said Perry was being understandably cautious on any new force, "but the White House people just look at everything in a political sense."

"It's clear that nothing will happen without us (United States," added Pirnie. "They don't want to talk about it, but the most important thing here is to make sure enough troops are sent so that the cutthroats there are not tempted to challenge them."

The New York Times last week quoted a senior European diplomat as saying that although the United States had not specifically said it would put U.S. troops on the ground next year, "there are nods and winks."
The Pentagon insists that nothing will be decided until NATO military planners and the North Atlantic Council, the alliance's political arm, resolve what any new force can - and should - do.
"A lot of people say a new IFOR is a fact, that the only way to keep peace is to send a new posse. But we are not going to jump until the mission is clear," a senior defence official told Reuters.
Even as it begins withdrawing 15,000 troops, however, the United States is sending more than 5,000 into Bosnia from Germany to cover the withdrawal and remain until at least mid-March.
That date is already far beyond this year's December 20 deadline set by Clinton and other western leaders for withdrawing IFOR under the Dayton agreement.
Perry, at a recent rancorous Congressional hearing, denied that the U.S. covering force is designed as the vanguard of a follow-on to IFOR.

Perry on Saturday issued an unusual public statement denying the thrust of a New York Times report that quoted administration officials, NATO leaders and European diplomats as saying "active planning" was under way for a force of 15,000 to 30,000 troops that would remain in Bosnia at least through 1997.
He said NATO military advisers were considering four options they would present soon to the North Atlantic Council and that no decision had been made by the alliance or the United States.

The options are complete withdrawal of the current NATO force, a "deterrence force" to prevent outbreak of fighting, a "sustaining force" to provide security for civilians in Bosnia, and a continuation of the current mission.

Perry has previously said that only the first three options were viable and that the deterrence force might not even require any troops on the ground, instead stationing them outside Bosnia to swoop in and quash any new outbreak of war.
